title: A1 consolidation
objectives: I can introduce myself in detail and make small talk about my work, studies, home and plans.
I can handle simple situations such as asking for help, getting directions, shopping and making plans.
I can ask for repetition or clarification when I do not understand.
I can connect sentences with e, mas, porque, então, também and por isso, and avoid common beginner errors.
I can explain why each word in this unit is written, accented and pronounced as it is, and tell a literal meaning from a natural translation.

vocabulary.note: Said to pass someone, to interrupt, or to enter a room. Licença is permission, as in a driving license or a leave of absence, so the phrase asks 'with your permission'. It is not an apology: after a mistake you say desculpa. Spelling: the ç keeps the s sound before a (li-CEN-sa), the en is nasal, and the o of com is nasal because of the m.

example.target: Com licença, onde fica o banheiro?
example.source: Excuse me, where is the bathroom?
example.source_literal: With license, where stays the bathroom?

vocabulary.note: Entendi is the past tense of entender. A tense says when an action happens, and the past tense says it was finished before now. English adds did and keeps the verb plain (I did not understand); Portuguese changes the ending of the verb itself (entend-er, entend-i, 'I understood'). The full past tense is taught at A2; here the form is a fixed phrase. Não entendo, in the present, means 'I do not understand (in general)', while não entendi means 'I did not get that just now'. Spelling: it ends in i, so the last syllable is stressed by default and no accent is needed (en-ten-DI), and d before i is said like English j.

example.target: Desculpa, eu não entendi.
example.source: Sorry, I didn't understand.

vocabulary.note: Fala is the form you already know for você (você fala), used here as a casual command, which is how Brazilians usually ask. The textbook command form is fale. Por favor is literally 'by favor'. Devagar is an adverb, so it never changes for gender or number.

example.target: Você fala muito rápido. Fala mais devagar, por favor.
example.source: You speak very fast. Speak more slowly, please.

vocabulary.note: Pode is the você form of poder, 'to be able'. The subject você is left out because the verb already shows who is meant, and poder is followed directly by an infinitive with no word for 'to' in between. Pode ends in e, so the default stress is on the second to last syllable (PO-de) and there is no accent. Pôde, with a circumflex, is a different word, the past tense 'was able'.

example.target: Pode repetir, por favor?
example.source: Can you repeat, please?

vocabulary.note: Me is an object pronoun, a small word that stands for the person who receives the action. In Brazilian speech it goes before the verb, the same place as the reflexive me of eu me levanto, but here it is not reflexive: it means 'me', not 'myself'. The full set of object pronouns is taught at A2. In ajudar the j is always the zh sound of the s in 'measure'.

example.target: Com licença, pode me ajudar?
example.source: Excuse me, can you help me?

vocabulary.note: Here se is impersonal: it makes the question about people in general ('how does one say it?') rather than about one particular person. In the reflexive verbs of the daily routine lesson, the same se meant himself or herself (ela se veste). English uses 'you', 'one' or a passive (how is it said?) where Portuguese uses se. Spelling: the z of diz is said like s at the end of a word, and d before i is said like English j, so diz sounds like 'jees'.

example.target: Como se diz obrigado em inglês?
example.source: How do you say obrigado in English?

vocabulary.note: O que, two words, is 'what'. Significa is the third person singular of significar. Unlike English, Portuguese has no helper verb here (English says 'does... mean'). Spelling: g is soft only before e or i, so the g of sig-ni-fi-ca, which is followed by n, is the hard g of 'go'. The stress is on fi, the default for a word ending in a.

example.target: O que significa essa palavra?
example.source: What does this word mean?

vocabulary.note: The impersonal se again. Escrever is 'to write', and Portuguese uses it for spelling a word. The same question also means 'how is it written?'. Spelling: the c before r is k (es-CRE-ve), and the stress is on cre, the default for a word ending in e.

example.target: Como se escreve o seu nome?
example.source: How do you spell your name?

vocabulary.note: Perdido is an adjective made from the verb perder, 'to lose'. As an adjective it agrees with the speaker: a man says perdido and a woman says perdida. It takes estar because being lost describes a condition, not what you are. The d before i is said like English j (per-JEE-do).

example.target: Com licença, eu estou perdido.
example.source: Excuse me, I'm lost.

vocabulary.target: Eu falo um pouco de português.
vocabulary.source_literal: I speak a little of Portuguese.
vocabulary.note: Um pouco is followed by de before the thing: 'a little of'. In pouco, ou is a diphthong. Português ends in es, whose default is the second to last syllable, but the stress is on the last, so it is written with a circumflex (por-tu-GUÊS, closed e). Language names are not capitalized in Portuguese.

example.target: Eu falo um pouco de português, mas estudo todo dia.
example.source: I speak a little Portuguese, but I study every day.

vocabulary.note: An adverb is a word that adds information to a verb, and it does not change for gender or number. Spelling: it ends in r, whose default is the last syllable, so de-va-GAR needs no accent.

example.target: A minha avó fala devagar.
example.source: My grandmother speaks slowly.

vocabulary.note: Novo is 'new', and de novo works like English 'anew': doing something again from the start. The stressed o of novo is a closed o (the plural novos has an open one), but no mark shows it, because a written accent only marks stress that breaks the default; you learn the vowel quality by ear.

example.target: Pode falar de novo, por favor?
example.source: Can you say that again, please?
example.source_literal: Can speak of new, by favor?

vocabulary.note: A conjunction is a word that joins two clauses, and mas joins two clauses that contrast. It is a small unstressed word, so it has no accent. Do not confuse it with mais, 'more', which has an i.

example.target: Eu quero ir, mas não posso.
example.source: I want to go, but I can't.

vocabulary.note: Built from por, 'for', and que, 'what', and written as one word when it gives a reason. Spelling: qu before e is the k sound and the u is silent. For the three other spellings of 'why' (por que, por quê, porquê) see the note on questions.

example.target: Eu estudo português porque gosto do Brasil.
example.source: I study Portuguese because I like Brazil.

vocabulary.note: Two words when it asks for a reason. The answer begins with porque, one word. At the very end of a question it is written por quê, with a circumflex, because que is then stressed.

example.target: Por que você estuda português?
example.source: Why do you study Portuguese?

vocabulary.note: Spelling: the en is a nasal vowel and ão is a nasal diphthong. It ends in ão, whose default is the last syllable, so en-TÃO breaks no rule; the tilde marks the nasal sound and also the stress, so no other accent is added. It gives a result (so) or moves a conversation on (well, then).

example.target: Está chovendo, então eu fico em casa.
example.source: It is raining, so I stay home.

vocabulary.note: Spelling: a word ending in em is normally stressed on the second to last syllable, but this one is said tam-BÉM, so the last syllable carries an acute accent. The m of tam and the final m both make the vowel nasal. Também goes before the verb (eu também gosto, 'I also like') or at the end (eu gosto também, 'I like it too'); também não means 'neither'.

example.target: Eu também gosto de futebol.
example.source: I like soccer too.

vocabulary.note: Isso is the demonstrative 'that'. It points back to what was just said, so the sentence with por isso gives the result of the sentence before it. Spelling: ss between vowels is always the s sound, while a single s between vowels would be z.

example.target: Está frio, por isso eu uso casaco.
example.source: It is cold, that is why I wear a coat.
example.source_literal: Is cold, for this I use coat.

vocabulary.note: Spelling: before a, the u of qu is pronounced as a quick w, so it is KWAN-do. The an is a nasal vowel because the n ends its syllable. Quando is both a question word and a conjunction (quando eu chego, 'when I arrive').

example.target: Quando você vai viajar?
example.source: When are you going to travel?

vocabulary.note: It agrees with the noun it counts: quantos, quantas. Spelling: qu before a is KW. Portuguese asks age with ter, so quantos anos você tem? is literally 'how many years do you have?'.

example.target: Quantos anos você tem?
example.source: How old are you?

vocabulary.note: Ainda não means 'not yet', and ainda alone means 'still'. Spelling: a-IN-da. The i is stressed and starts a new syllable after the a, but it is followed by n in the same syllable, so no accent is needed on the i (compare aí and país, where the i stands alone and is marked). The stress is the default for a word ending in a.

example.target: Eu ainda não falo bem.
example.source: I don't speak well yet.

vocabulary.note: Spelling: a stressed one-syllable word that ends in a, e or o takes an accent, as in já, é, pé and só.

example.target: Eu já conheço o bairro.
example.source: I already know the neighborhood.

vocabulary.note: Used for taking transport (pegar o ônibus), for picking something up, and for catching an illness. Spelling: g is hard before a and o (pegar, eu pego); before e it must be written gu to stay hard (pegue).

example.target: Eu pego o metrô todo dia.
example.source: I take the subway every day.
example.source_literal: I grab the subway every day.

vocabulary.note: Conhecer means to be acquainted with a person or place, and to meet someone for the first time. Saber, in contrast, is for facts and skills (eu sei nadar). Spelling: nh is the ny sound, ce is the s sound, and in the first person the c becomes ç to keep that sound before o: eu conheço.

example.target: Eu conheço bem o centro.
example.source: I know downtown well.

vocabulary.note: With se it is reciprocal, meaning each other: a gente se encontra, 'we meet'. Without se it means 'to find'. Spelling: en is nasal because the n ends the syllable.

example.target: A gente se encontra às oito.
example.source: We meet at eight.

vocabulary.note: A false friend: legal means 'lawful' and, in everyday speech, 'cool' or 'great'. Que before an adjective makes an exclamation, as in Que bom! and Que caro!. Spelling: a final l is said like w, so it is le-GAW.

example.target: Você mora no Rio? Que legal!
example.source: You live in Rio? How cool!
example.source_literal: You live in-the Rio? What legal!

vocabulary.note: Mesmo is 'same', and as an adverb it means 'really, indeed'. Said with rising intonation it shows surprise or interest. Spelling: é is a stressed one-syllable word ending in e, so it has an accent, which also separates é, 'is', from e, 'and'. The s before the voiced consonant m is said z (ME-zmo).

example.target: Eu moro em Belém. É mesmo? Eu também!
example.source: I live in Belém. Really? Me too!

vocabulary.note: Pois is an old conjunction meaning 'since' or 'so'; the phrase has become a stock reaction that agrees with what was said, often with a shrug, as in 'yes, that is how it is'. Only the usage explains it; the literal words do not.

example.target: Está muito caro. Pois é.
example.source: It's very expensive. Yeah, I know.

dialogues.title: Fazendo amizade
dialogues.context: Tom, an American, is new in São Paulo. He meets Carol, a Brazilian university student, in a café. They do small talk.

lines.speaker: Carol
lines.target: Oi! Você é novo aqui? Eu sou a Carol.
lines.source: Hi! Are you new here? I'm Carol.
lines.source_literal: Hi! You are new here? I am the Carol.

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.target: Oi, Carol! Eu sou o Tom. Sou dos Estados Unidos, mas agora moro em São Paulo.
lines.source: Hi, Carol! I'm Tom. I'm from the United States, but now I live in São Paulo.
lines.source_literal: Hi, Carol! I am the Tom. I-am of-the States United, but now I-live in São Paulo.

lines.speaker: Carol
lines.target: Que legal! Você trabalha ou estuda?
lines.source: How cool! Do you work or study?
lines.source_literal: What legal! You work or study?

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.target: Eu trabalho num banco, de segunda a sexta. E você?
lines.source: I work in a bank, Monday to Friday. And you?
lines.source_literal: I work in-a bank, from second to sixth. And you?

lines.speaker: Carol
lines.target: Eu estudo medicina. Tenho vinte e dois anos. E você?
lines.source: I study medicine. I'm twenty-two. And you?
lines.source_literal: I study medicine. I-have twenty and two years. And you?

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.target: Tenho vinte e oito. Eu falo um pouco de português, mas ainda não entendo tudo.
lines.source: I'm twenty-eight. I speak a little Portuguese, but I don't understand everything yet.
lines.source_literal: I-have twenty and eight. I speak a little of Portuguese, but still not I-understand everything.

lines.speaker: Carol
lines.target: Seu português é ótimo! Vou falar mais devagar, tá?
lines.source: Your Portuguese is great! I'll speak more slowly, okay?
lines.source_literal: Your Portuguese is great! I-go to-speak more slow, is?

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.target: Obrigado! Você mora perto daqui?
lines.source: Thank you! Do you live near here?
lines.source_literal: Obliged! You live near of-here?

lines.speaker: Carol
lines.target: Moro, sim. Tem um parque na minha rua. Nos fins de semana eu jogo futebol lá.
lines.source: Yes, I do. There's a park on my street. On weekends I play soccer there.
lines.source_literal: I-live, yes. Has a park on-the my street. In-the ends of week I play soccer there.

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.target: Eu gosto de futebol! Você joga todo domingo?
lines.source: I like soccer! Do you play every Sunday?
lines.source_literal: I like of soccer! You play every Sunday?

lines.speaker: Carol
lines.target: Jogo, sim. Domingo eu vou jogar com os amigos. Você quer ir?
lines.source: Yes, I do. On Sunday I'm going to play with friends. Do you want to go?
lines.source_literal: I-play, yes. Sunday I go to-play with the friends. You want to-go?

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.target: Com certeza! Que horas?
lines.source: Of course! What time?
lines.source_literal: With certainty! What hours?

lines.speaker: Carol
lines.target: Às nove, no parque, em frente à igreja.
lines.source: At nine, in the park, across from the church.
lines.source_literal: At-the nine, in-the park, in front at-the church.

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.target: Combinado! Até domingo!
lines.source: Deal! See you Sunday!
lines.source_literal: Arranged! Until Sunday!

dialogues.title: Perdido na cidade
dialogues.context: Tom is lost in his neighborhood. He asks Dona Lúcia on the street for directions, and then goes into the pharmacy to buy sunscreen from the pharmacist, Rafael.

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.target: Com licença, eu estou perdido. Onde fica a farmácia?
lines.source: Excuse me, I'm lost. Where is the pharmacy?
lines.source_literal: With license, I am lost. Where stays the pharmacy?

lines.speaker: Lúcia
lines.target: Fica na Rua das Flores. Você segue em frente e vira na segunda rua à direita.
lines.source: It's on Flores Street. You go straight ahead and turn onto the second street on the right.
lines.source_literal: Stays on-the Street of-the Flowers. You follow in front and turn on-the second street to-the right.

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.target: Desculpa, não entendi. Pode falar mais devagar?
lines.source: Sorry, I didn't understand. Can you speak more slowly?
lines.source_literal: Excuse, not I-understood. Can speak more slow?

lines.speaker: Lúcia
lines.target: Claro. Siga em frente. Depois vire à direita, na segunda rua.
lines.source: Of course. Go straight ahead. Then turn right, onto the second street.
lines.source_literal: Clear. Follow in front. Afterwards turn to-the right, on-the second street.

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.target: Siga em frente e vire na segunda rua à direita. Isso?
lines.source: Go straight ahead and turn onto the second street on the right. Right?
lines.source_literal: Follow in front and turn on-the second street to-the right. That?

lines.speaker: Lúcia
lines.target: Isso! A farmácia fica ao lado do banco.
lines.source: That's it! The pharmacy is next to the bank.
lines.source_literal: That! The pharmacy stays at-the side of-the bank.

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.target: Muito obrigado! Eu moro aqui, mas conheço pouco o bairro.
lines.source: Thank you very much! I live here, but I don't know the neighborhood much.
lines.source_literal: Very obliged! I live here, but I-know little the neighborhood.

lines.speaker: Lúcia
lines.target: De nada. Boa sorte!
lines.source: You're welcome. Good luck!
lines.source_literal: Of nothing. Good luck!

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.target: Boa tarde! Quanto custa esse protetor solar?
lines.source: Good afternoon! How much does this sunscreen cost?
lines.source_literal: Good afternoon! How-much costs this protector solar?

lines.speaker: Rafael
lines.target: Custa quarenta e cinco reais.
lines.source: It costs forty-five reais.
lines.source_literal: Costs forty and five reais.

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.target: Que caro! Vocês aceitam Pix?
lines.source: That's expensive! Do you accept Pix?
lines.source_literal: What expensive! You-all accept Pix?

lines.speaker: Rafael
lines.target: Aceitamos, sim. Cartão também.
lines.source: Yes, we do. Cards too.
lines.source_literal: We-accept, yes. Card also.

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.target: Eu pago com Pix. Obrigado!
lines.source: I'll pay with Pix. Thanks!
lines.source_literal: I pay with Pix. Obliged!

dialogues.title: O apartamento novo
dialogues.context: Marina has a new apartment. She invites her friend Caio to visit on Saturday.

lines.speaker: Marina
lines.target: Caio, você quer conhecer o meu apartamento novo?
lines.source: Caio, do you want to see my new apartment?
lines.source_literal: Caio, you want to-know the my apartment new?

lines.speaker: Caio
lines.target: Quero! Onde fica?
lines.source: I do! Where is it?
lines.source_literal: I-want! Where stays?

lines.speaker: Marina
lines.target: Perto do metrô, no quarto andar.
lines.source: Near the subway, on the fourth floor.
lines.source_literal: Near of-the subway, on-the fourth floor.

lines.speaker: Caio
lines.target: Legal! Quantos quartos tem?
lines.source: Nice! How many bedrooms does it have?
lines.source_literal: Legal! How-many bedrooms has?

lines.speaker: Marina
lines.target: Tem dois quartos e uma varanda pequena, mas é muito claro.
lines.source: It has two bedrooms and a small balcony, but it is very bright.
lines.source_literal: Has two bedrooms and a balcony small, but is very clear.

lines.speaker: Caio
lines.target: E o aluguel? É caro?
lines.source: And the rent? Is it expensive?

lines.speaker: Marina
lines.target: É mil e oitocentos reais. É caro, mas o bairro é tranquilo.
lines.source: It's one thousand eight hundred reais. It's expensive, but the neighborhood is quiet.
lines.source_literal: Is thousand and eight-hundred reais. Is expensive, but the neighborhood is quiet.

lines.speaker: Caio
lines.target: Quando eu posso ir?
lines.source: When can I go?

lines.speaker: Marina
lines.target: No sábado à tarde. Vai fazer sol, então a gente toma um café na varanda.
lines.source: On Saturday afternoon. It's going to be sunny, so we'll have coffee on the balcony.
lines.source_literal: On-the Saturday at-the afternoon. Goes to-make sun, then the-people takes a coffee on-the balcony.

lines.speaker: Caio
lines.target: Perfeito! De manhã eu preciso trabalhar, mas depois estou livre.
lines.source: Perfect! In the morning I need to work, but afterwards I'm free.
lines.source_literal: Perfect! Of morning I need to-work, but afterwards I-am free.

lines.speaker: Marina
lines.target: Então a gente se encontra às três. Você sabe chegar?
lines.source: Then we'll meet at three. Do you know how to get there?
lines.source_literal: Then the-people meets-itself at-the three. You know to-arrive?

lines.speaker: Caio
lines.target: Eu pego o metrô e chego em quinze minutos.
lines.source: I take the subway and get there in fifteen minutes.
lines.source_literal: I grab the subway and I-arrive in fifteen minutes.

lines.speaker: Marina
lines.target: Isso! Até sábado!
lines.source: Right! See you Saturday!
lines.source_literal: That! Until Saturday!

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: accents and stress in this unit's words
grammar.explanation:
Every accent mark in this unit's words follows from the lesson on stress and accent marks, so this note applies that lesson instead of adding new rules. Recall the principle. By default, a word ending in a, e or o (with or without a final s), or in am, em or ens, is stressed on the second to last syllable, and a word ending in anything else is stressed on the last syllable. A written accent appears when a word breaks the default of its ending, and it sits on the stressed vowel. So an accent is never decoration: it says that this word is an exception to its ending, and the absence of an accent says that the default applies.

Try it on the longer words. Também ends in em, whose default is the second to last syllable, but the word is said tam-BÉM, so the last syllable is marked with an acute accent. Português and até break their endings in the same way, and so does metrô, which takes a circumflex because its o is closed. Devagar ends in r, whose default is the last syllable, so de-va-GAR needs no mark, and neither does entendi, which ends in i. Então ends in ão, whose default is also the last syllable, so it breaks nothing; the tilde is there because ão is a nasal diphthong, and it happens to mark the stress as well. Sábado, farmácia and Lúcia are stressed on the third to last syllable, which no ending predicts, so they are always marked. The ia at the end counts as two syllables, which is why far-MÁ-ci-a has its stress third from the end.

One-syllable words follow a separate rule. A one-syllable word that is stressed and ends in a, e or o (with or without s) takes an accent: já, é, tá, lá, nós, três, pé. A one-syllable word that is a small helper, spoken without stress, takes none: mas, que, de, se, me, com, por, e, o, a. This is why é, 'is', has an accent and e, 'and', does not; why tá is written with one (it is a clipped form of está); and why que has no accent inside a sentence while quê has one at the end of a question. In 'por quê?' the stress falls on quê, just as it does on pé.

Three more groups of marked words appear in the dialogues. First, proparoxytones, words stressed on the third to last syllable: ótimo (Ó-ti-mo), número (NÚ-me-ro), rápido (RÁ-pi-do) and sábado. No ending predicts that stress, so the accent is always written, and the vowel decides the mark: open ó and á take the acute, and u, which has only one quality, takes the acute as well. Second, the tilde words amanhã, irmãos, cartão and são. Endings ã, ão and ãos default to the last syllable, so the tilde never breaks the default here; it marks the nasal sound and, because there is no other accent, the stress as well: a-ma-NHÃ, ir-MÃOS, car-TÃO. Niterói is ni-te-RÓI: the stress is on the last syllable, which oi (an i ending) would default to anyway, but Portuguese writes the acute on a stressed open diphthong éi, éu or ói in the last syllable to show the open vowel, as in papéis and herói.

Third, the grave accent, which appears in à direita, à tarde and às três. It has one job, called crase. The preposition a (to, at) is a small word that links a verb to its destination or time, and the article a (the) is the small word before a feminine noun; when the two meet they fuse into one long a, written à, and with the plural article as they fuse into às. The grave only records the fusion. It does not change the stress or the sound. A test: if the masculine version of the phrase would use ao, the feminine one takes à (vou ao mercado, vou à praia).

Last, the hiatus, which is two vowels pronounced in separate syllables. In aí (a-Í) the stressed i is alone in its syllable, so it is marked. In ainda (a-IN-da) the stressed i is followed by n in the same syllable, so no mark is needed, and the stress is simply the default for a word ending in a. On oral vowels the acute and circumflex also tell you the quality of the vowel: the acute is open (é, já), and the circumflex is closed (você, três, metrô). Before m or n the vowel is nasal, and the acute in também is only the spelling convention for words ending in em.

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: letters and sound patterns in this unit
grammar.explanation:
Portuguese spelling is a code in which the letters next to a letter often decide how it is said, so most surprises come from a few rules in the lesson on sounds. Six of them cover the words of this unit.

The cedilla. The letter c is said k before a, o and u, and s before e and i. When the s sound is needed before a, o or u, the c takes a cedilla: ç. So licença is li-CEN-sa. The verb conhecer shows why the rule matters. Its stem conhec- ends in the s sound, and before the ending -o a plain c would turn into the k sound, so the first person is written conheço, not conheco. The other forms (conhece, conhecemos) keep a plain c because e already gives s.

The letters qu and gu. Before e or i the u is normally silent and only keeps the hard sound: que and porque are said with k, and segue with a hard g. A few words are exceptions in which the u is said (tranquilo, cinquenta), so those are learned individually. Before a or o the u is a quick w: quando is KWAN-do and quantos is KWAN-tos.

Nasal vowels. A vowel followed by m or n in the same syllable is said through the nose, and the m or n is not pronounced as a separate consonant: en-ten-di, tam-bém, quan-do, com-bi-na-do and com are all nasal. The tilde does the same job in não, então and cartão.

T and d before i. In most of Brazil, d before the sound i (an i, or a weak final e) is said like English j, and t is said like English ch. So entendi ends in 'jee', diz is 'jees', the small word de is 'jee', and vinte ends in 'chee'.

The letter s. Between two vowels, and before a voiced consonant such as m, it is said z: me-zmo, casa. A double ss is always s: isso. At the start of a word it is s, and the x of sexta, before a consonant, is s as well. A final x, as in Pix, is ks, like the x of táxi.

The letter l and the digraphs. At the end of a syllable, l is said w: legal is le-GAW, mil is [miw], aluguel is a-lu-GÉW. A digraph is a pair of letters that stands for one sound: nh is ny (conhecer), ch is sh (chego), and the single letter j is always zh (igreja, ajudar).

grammar.title: Literal meaning, natural English and usage
grammar.explanation:
Every expression has three layers, and this course keeps them apart. The literal meaning is what the words say, one by one, in Portuguese word order. The natural English is what an English speaker would say in the same situation. The usage is who says it, when, and in which register, meaning how formal or casual it is. The layers often differ, because every language fixes its own idioms. English says 'excuse me' and Portuguese says com licença, literally 'with license'. Neither is wrong; they are two ways of making the same social move, and translating word by word is what produces unnatural sentences in both directions.

Use the layers for different jobs. Use the natural English to know what a sentence means and what to say. Use the literal meaning to see how the language is built and to remember it: licença is permission, as in a driving license or a leave of absence, so com licença asks 'with your permission' to pass or to interrupt. It is not an apology. When you have made a mistake, you say desculpa.

Three patterns explain most of the differences. First, Portuguese builds the idea with a different verb or structure: tenho trinta anos is 'I have thirty years', estou com fome is 'I am with hunger', and gosto de café is 'I like of coffee'. Second, Portuguese has a fixed phrase where English has another: de nada is 'of nothing', por favor is 'by favor', com certeza is 'with certainty', que horas? is 'what hours?', and até sábado is 'until Saturday', which means 'see you then'. Third, a word can look like an English word and behave differently. Legal is 'lawful' and, in speech, 'cool'. Words like this are called false friends.

Some literal meanings are only partly clear, such as pois é. Pois is an old conjunction meaning 'since' or 'so', and the phrase has become a stock reaction. In that case the literal gloss shows the parts and the usage explains the rest. When a phrase is already word for word the same as English, as with o livro, 'the book', there is nothing to separate.

grammar.title: Review: the four key verbs and the present tense
grammar.explanation:
A Portuguese verb ending carries the subject: falo can only mean 'I speak', and fala can mean he, she, you or one speaks. English verbs hardly change (I speak, she speaks), so English must say the pronoun; Portuguese lets the ending do that work, which is why subject pronouns are often dropped. A verb is learned as its infinitive, the dictionary form (falar, comer, abrir), and the last two letters of the infinitive (-ar, -er, -ir) say which of three regular patterns of endings it follows.

The regular endings of the present tense are -o, -a, -amos, -am for -ar verbs (falar: falo, fala, falamos, falam); -o, -e, -emos, -em for -er verbs (comer); and -o, -e, -imos, -em for -ir verbs (abrir). The form for você, ele, ela and a gente is the same, and so is the form for vocês, eles and elas. That sameness is why the table below needs only four rows for nine pronouns, and why a gente, which means 'we' in speech, takes a third person singular verb.

Four verbs are irregular: ser, estar, ter and ir. They are irregular because they are the most frequent verbs in the language, and frequent words resist regularization in every language; English am, is, are and go, went are irregular for the same reason. Portuguese has two verbs where English has one 'to be'. Ser says what something is: identity, origin, profession, defining traits (eu sou brasileiro, ela é professora). Estar says where something is, or what condition it is in at the moment (eu estou em casa, ele está cansado). Permanent versus temporary is a useful guide, not the rule: what decides is whether you name what something is or describe its condition. Ter means to have; it also expresses age (eu tenho trinta anos, literally 'I have thirty years') and, in the form tem, 'there is' and 'there are'. Ir means to go, and ir followed by an infinitive makes the near future (eu vou viajar), as 'going to' does in English.

Three more pieces complete the system. Reflexive verbs, which describe an action done to oneself, put the small pronoun before the verb in Brazil: eu me levanto. Contractions are compulsory: the preposition and the article fuse, so em + o is no, de + a is da, a + o is ao and por + o is pelo; English 'in the' stays two words, but Portuguese writes one. And after poder, querer, ir and precisar, a second verb stays in the infinitive with nothing between them: pode repetir, vou falar, quero ir. Some other verbs add a small word first, as in gosto de dançar and tenho que sair.

grammar.title: Review: asking questions
grammar.explanation:
A question asks for information. English builds questions with the helper verb do (Do you live here? Where does she work?), which moves in front of the subject. Portuguese has no such helper and moves nothing. A yes-or-no question is the plain statement said with rising intonation and written with a question mark: você mora aqui? A tag such as né? ('right?') can be added at the end. Né is the contraction of não é, 'is it not', and it has an accent because it is a stressed one-syllable word ending in e. An information question puts the question word first and keeps the statement order: onde você mora? quando a festa começa?

The question words each ask for one kind of information: quem (a person), o que (a thing), qual (a choice from a set, so 'which', and also 'what' in qual é o seu número?), onde (a place), quando (a time), como (a manner), por que (a reason) and quanto (an amount). Qual becomes quais in the plural, the same l-to-is change as in animal and animais. Quanto agrees with the noun it counts: quantos anos, quantas pessoas. When it asks about a verb (quanto custa?) it stays quanto.

The word 'why' has four spellings, and each has a job. Por que, two words, begins a question, and is literally 'for what': por que você estuda português? Porque, one word, begins the answer: porque eu gosto do Brasil. At the end of a sentence the question becomes por quê, with a circumflex, because que is then stressed and a stressed one-syllable word ending in e takes an accent: você não vem? Por quê? As a noun, 'the reason', it is porquê, one word with an accent: não sei o porquê.

Requests use the same plain structure. Pode followed by an infinitive asks politely: pode repetir? is literally 'can repeat?', with the subject você understood. To ask about words, Portuguese uses se. In the reflexive verbs of the daily routine, se meant himself or herself (ela se veste). With a verb in the third person singular and no particular subject, the same se makes the action general: como se diz...? is literally 'how says-itself?', meaning 'how does one say it?'. English uses 'one', 'you' or a passive (how is it said?) where Portuguese uses se. So como se escreve...? asks how a word is spelled, and o que significa...? asks for its meaning.

grammar.title: Common beginner errors
grammar.explanation:
A beginner error is usually a correct English habit applied to Portuguese. Each correction below follows from a rule taught earlier, so learn the rule and not only the corrected sentence.

Ser and estar. English has one verb 'to be'; Portuguese splits the job. Use ser to say what something is (identity, origin, profession, a defining trait) and estar to say where it is or what condition it is in. So eu estou cansado (my condition now) but ela é professora (what she is). Permanent versus temporary is a guide, not the rule: ele está morto, 'he is dead', uses estar even though death is permanent, because it describes a condition.

Age. English says 'I am thirty'. Portuguese says 'I have thirty years': eu tenho trinta anos, and the question is quantos anos você tem?

Gender and agreement. Gender belongs to the noun, not to its meaning, and the ending is only a guide. Many nouns of Greek origin that end in -ma, such as problema, tema and sistema, are masculine: o problema. Adjectives copy the gender and number of the noun: uma casa pequena, dois quartos pequenos.

Contractions. Before an article, write the fused form: no, not em o; da, not de a. English keeps 'in the' as two words, and Portuguese does not.

Tem and têm. The plural of ter is têm, with a circumflex. The circumflex does not change the sound in Brazil, because tem and têm are said alike; it exists only to tell singular from plural, which is a differential accent. The tem that means 'there is' or 'there are' has no subject to agree with, so it is always tem, even before a plural noun: tem dois quartos. Têm needs a plural subject: eles têm dois quartos. The formal way to say 'there is' and 'there are' is há, from haver, which is also invariable. It has an accent because it is a stressed one-syllable word ending in a, and the accent also keeps it apart from the preposition a.

Muito. After a verb, or before an adjective, muito is an adverb, and an adverb does not agree: eu gosto muito de café. Before a noun it is an adjective and agrees: muitos amigos, muita gente.

Negatives. When a negative word follows the verb, Portuguese requires não before the verb as well: eu não como carne nunca. If nunca comes before the verb, não is dropped: eu nunca como carne.

grammar.title: Connecting sentences: e, mas, porque, então
grammar.explanation:
A clause is a group of words built around one verb: eu trabalho is a clause. A sentence can be one clause, or several joined by a conjunction, a word whose job is to join. Two kinds of joining matter. Coordination joins two clauses of equal weight: e (and), mas (but, a contrast) and ou (or, a choice). Subordination makes one clause depend on another: porque (because), que (that) and quando (when). Portuguese uses the same two groups as English, so the work here is learning the words and their direction.

Cause and result use mirror-image words. Porque introduces the reason, and the reason comes second: eu fico em casa porque está chovendo. Então and por isso introduce the result, and the result comes second: está chovendo, então eu fico em casa. Por isso is literally 'for this', pointing back to what was just said. Então is softer: 'then, in that case'. So choose by direction. If you are giving the reason, use porque; if you are giving the consequence, use então or por isso.

Some small adverbs, words that add information to a verb, order events and show time. Depois (afterwards), antes (before) and primeiro (first) order events: primeiro eu trabalho, depois eu estudo. Ainda means 'still' and, with não, 'not yet': eu ainda não falo bem. Já means 'already': eu já conheço o bairro. Também means 'also' and goes before the verb or at the end of the clause: eu também gosto, eu gosto também. Também não means 'neither': eu não falo inglês, eu também não.

Two cautions. Mas, 'but', and mais, 'more', are different words; mas has no i. And in speech Brazilians often begin a sentence with então or aí, which work like 'so' or 'and then' in English and keep the conversation moving: então, o que você vai fazer? The aí has an accent because its stressed i stands alone in its syllable after the a. Keep your sentences short at this level and join them with these words.

culture.title: Speaking Portuguese with Brazilians
culture.text:
Brazilians are usually warm and patient with people who are learning Portuguese. They will often help with a word, repeat something more slowly or switch to a simpler way of saying it, especially if you say eu falo um pouco de português and smile. Do not be afraid of mistakes: effort is appreciated, and people would rather have a conversation than correct your grammar.

Small talk starts quickly and can be more personal than in English-speaking countries. You will often hear questions about your family, your job, whether you are married, and whether you like Brazil and Brazilian food. Common conversation fillers are né ('right?', a contraction of não é, literally 'is it not'), tá ('okay', a clipped form of está, literally 'is'), beleza ('all good', literally 'beauty'), pois é ('yeah, exactly', literally 'since is') and nossa ('wow', short for Nossa Senhora, literally 'Our Lady'). In the south of Brazil and in Rio, tu is also used in casual speech, but você works everywhere.

A few habits are worth learning early. Greet people with a handshake or a light kiss on the cheek among friends. Say com licença, literally 'with license', meaning 'with your permission', when you pass through a crowd or interrupt, and keep desculpa for when you have actually made a mistake. Use moço or moça, in which the ç keeps the s sound before o and a, to call a stranger politely. Being late by a few minutes is normal for social plans, although you should be on time for work. If you do not understand, the best survival phrases are não entendi, pode repetir, por favor? and fala mais devagar, por favor.
